title: Coplanar Vector
notes:
Definition

Vectors lying on the same plane are called coplanar vectors.

Examples

  • Three vectors drawn on the same flat sheet of paper
examples:
**Q1: Define coplanar vectors.**

**Answer:** Vectors lying on the same plane.

**Q2: Can coplanar vectors have different magnitudes and directions?**

**Answer:** Yes, the only requirement is that they lie in the same plane.

**Q3: Are two vectors always coplanar?**

**Answer:** Yes, any two vectors can always be contained within some common plane.

**Q4: When does the concept of coplanarity become meaningful?**

**Answer:** When dealing with three or more vectors, since two vectors are always trivially coplanar.

**Q5: Give an example of three coplanar vectors.**

**Answer:** Three force vectors all lying flat on a table's surface.

**Q6: Give an example of vectors that are NOT coplanar.**

**Answer:** Three mutually perpendicular vectors along x, y, and z axes (3D, non-coplanar).

**Q7: Are î and ĵ coplanar?**

**Answer:** Yes, they lie in the xy-plane.

**Q8: Are î, ĵ, and k̂ coplanar?**

**Answer:** No, they span three dimensions and are not coplanar.

**Q9: How is coplanarity of vectors tested mathematically (for 3 vectors)?**

**Answer:** Using the scalar triple product; if it equals zero, the vectors are coplanar.

**Q10: Is the concept of coplanar vectors related to the short-answer question about three vectors summing to zero?**

**Answer:** Yes, if the resultant of three coplanar vectors is zero, the third vector must balance the resultant of the other two, all lying in the same plane.

**Q11: Give a real-world example of coplanar forces.**

**Answer:** Three forces acting on a flat signboard, all in the plane of the board.

**Q12: Can coplanar vectors be collinear as well?**

**Answer:** Yes, collinear vectors are a special case of coplanar vectors (lying along the same line within a plane).

**Q13: Is every set of collinear vectors automatically coplanar?**

**Answer:** Yes, since a line lies within infinitely many planes, but specifically all collinear vectors share at least one common plane.

**Q14: Why is the coplanar condition important in structural mechanics?**

**Answer:** Because many equilibrium problems in 2D analysis assume all forces lie within a single plane.

**Q15: What geometric shape do 3 coplanar vectors typically form when added head-to-tail and returning to start?**

**Answer:** A closed triangle or polygon in that plane.

**Q16: If three coplanar forces are in equilibrium, what is their vector sum?**

**Answer:** Zero (null vector).

**Q17: Is the term 'coplanar' used only for vectors, or also for points and lines?**

**Answer:** It's a general geometric term applicable to points, lines, and vectors that lie within the same plane.

**Q18: Can four vectors be coplanar?**

**Answer:** Yes, any number of vectors can be coplanar if they all lie in the same plane.

**Q19: Give an example of two coplanar velocity vectors in projectile motion.**

**Answer:** Horizontal and vertical velocity components of a projectile, both lying in the vertical plane of motion.

**Q20: Is coplanarity a stricter or looser condition than collinearity?**

**Answer:** Looser — collinear vectors are always coplanar, but coplanar vectors need not be collinear.

**Q21: How would you show three given vectors A, B, C are coplanar using components?**

**Answer:** Show that A·(B×C) = 0 (scalar triple product is zero).

**Q22: Why are most basic vector addition problems (triangle/parallelogram law) implicitly assumed coplanar?**

**Answer:** Because triangle and parallelogram laws are 2D geometric constructions requiring the vectors to lie in one plane.

**Q23: Give a physics example where non-coplanar vectors must be considered.**

**Answer:** 3D motion analysis, such as a drone moving in x, y, and z directions simultaneously.

**Q24: If A and B lie in the xy-plane and C lies along the z-axis, are all three coplanar?**

**Answer:** No, C is not in the same plane as A and B.

**Q25: State one key application of coplanar vector concepts in exams.**

**Answer:** Solving equilibrium problems where all forces acting on a body lie in a single plane.
